newsitem.title: UK: UK advertising turns off women, survey shows.
newsitem.headline: UK advertising turns off women, survey shows.

text.p: Advertisers are failing to reach many women consumers in Britain because ads use old-fashioned stereotypes and ignore women's changing attitudes, a survey released on Wednesday said.
The survey "Women on the verge of the Millennium - how to win the new consumer", was published by Grey advertising agency and examined women's attitudes about work, family, friends and advertising.
"The housewife is well and truly dead," Nigel Sharrocks, managing director of Grey UK, said.
"Only one percent of the women we talked to said it was the role that described them best, whereas 86 per cent didn't think the term described them at all," he told reporters.
But Sharrocks said that many advertisers and ad agencies were failing to address the changing attitudes of women and that much of the advertising aimed at them was therefore irrelevant.

Of 220 women questioned, 61 per cent said that they found most advertising boring and repetitive, 37 per cent thought that most ads treat women as "idiots" and 32 per cent thought that most ads were "sexist".

The ads that women think work best are the ones that make them laugh. Among those that they like the most is an ad for Diet Coke which features women in the workplace watching a "hunky" workman taking off his clothes, an ad for Tesco Plc which features "imperfect" looking actresses and an ad for Oxo food flavouring which features an older woman with a sharp sense of humour.
The ads that they like least include those for detergent Fairy Liquid, for washing powder Daz and for Tampax tampons. Survey respondents said the ads presented stereotypical images of women.
Sharrocks said that in order to target women better, ads must be more relevant.

"Women live in the real world and would like to see their lives reflected in advertising. Nearly 90 per cent said that they would be interested in ads that show real women not actresses and models," he said.

"Women are not interested in being ultra thin and want ads that recognise that women don't want to look 18 forever. They want to see interesting attractive women who are also over 30 years old," Sharrocks said.
Grey is also studying the attitudes of women in the United States, Australia and across Europe. Next year it will look at the attitudes of Chinese female consumers.
